text:
## Observations

1. A die with \(K_i\) faces shows a number \(x\) with probability \(c_i(x)/K_i\), where \(c_i(x)\) is the number of faces labeled \(x\).
2. For two independently rolled dice, the probability of matching is the sum of the products of their probabilities for each shared label. Labels absent from either die contribute zero.
3. Each unordered pair of distinct dice needs to be evaluated once. Its match probability is an integer numerator divided by \(K_iK_j\).
4. If a die has \(D_i\) distinct labels, a pair can be evaluated with \(\min(D_i,D_j)\) dictionary lookups. The total number of distinct labels stored across the dice is at most the total number of faces.

## Solution sketch

> A die with \(K_i\) faces shows a number \(x\) with probability \(c_i(x)/K_i\), where \(c_i(x)\) is the number of faces labeled \(x\).

1. Read each die’s face count and build a dictionary mapping each label to its frequency. Count every occurrence of a repeated label. A one-face die produces a dictionary with a single entry of frequency one.

> For two independently rolled dice, the probability of matching is the sum of the products of their probabilities for each shared label. Labels absent from either die contribute zero.

2. For each pair with \(i<j\), iterate over the dictionary with fewer entries. For each label, multiply its frequency by the frequency in the other dictionary, using zero for a missing label. The sum of these products is the pair’s numerator, since all products share the denominator \(K_iK_j\). A pair with no shared labels has numerator zero.

> Each unordered pair of distinct dice needs to be evaluated once. Its match probability is an integer numerator divided by \(K_iK_j\).

3. Initialize the best fraction to \(0/1\) and compare each candidate with it by cross-multiplying integers. This keeps comparisons exact, including ties. After checking all pairs, divide the best numerator by its denominator and print the result to 15 decimal places, which meets the required tolerance. If every pair has probability zero, the initialized fraction gives the answer.

> If a die has \(D_i\) distinct labels, a pair can be evaluated with \(\min(D_i,D_j)\) dictionary lookups. The total number of distinct labels stored across the dice is at most the total number of faces.

4. Let \(S=\sum_i K_i\). Building the dictionaries takes expected \(O(S)\) time. Each die belongs to \(N-1\) pairs, so the total number of lookups is bounded by \((N-1)\sum_i D_i\). Since \(S\ge N\), the overall expected time is \(O(NS)\), including the overhead of enumerating pairs. Space usage is \(O(S)\).
